Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath
Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
I can't trust that I will do the right thing

issues.explanation: 'Arguments' is a weak fit as a primary trigger for PTSD related to a life-threatening illness when the rest of the profile is dominated by somatic danger cues, hypervigilant threat monitoring, and self-appraisals about coping. It is not impossible, but in this profile it appears disconnected from the illness-centered threat pattern and lacks support from memory/appraisal content.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: 'Restrict eating to feel in control' is not well integrated with the rest of the formulation. The active edges emphasize threat and negative appraisals leading to maladaptive strategies, but the other selected strategies are cognitive/self-punitive and illness-related themes are otherwise absent from eating control. In this profile it looks like a strategy addressing a different problem domain unless additional body/illness-control content were present.

vignette:
Moana came home from the hospital in late autumn, after seventeen days in the ICU for a rare bacterial pneumonia that had nearly stopped her breathing twice. She was a singer—had been since childhood, leading the church choir in her Samoan community, later performing with a local band on weekends—and the first thing she noticed when she walked through her front door was the way the air felt wrong. Not thin or heavy, just wrong, as though her lungs were listening for something that wasn't there. She stood in the kitchen, one hand on the counter, and waited for her chest to tighten. It did not. But she could not shake the feeling that it would.

In the months that followed, Moana learned to read her own body like a threat. A slight catch in her breath while climbing stairs sent her heart racing. The smell of antiseptic soap in a public restroom made her nauseous and alert, her palms sweating before she could name why. She began cancelling gigs that required long vocal sets, telling her bandmates she was still rebuilding her stamina. What she did not tell them was that she had started to believe she did not deserve to sing again—that the illness had been a kind of punishment for something she could not name, and that her survival meant she was simply postponing the real reckoning. The thought came to her most clearly at night: you got sick because you are not strong enough, and now you are a lousy coper because you cannot even breathe without panicking.

Her husband, Tanielu, noticed she would not let him drive past the hospital where she had been treated. She took a longer route to the grocery store. When her primary care physician called to schedule a follow-up, Moana said she would call back and never did. She told herself she was fine—her lungs had cleared on the last scan—but the idea of lying on an examination table, of someone pressing a stethoscope to her chest, filled her with a terror that felt older than thought. Her body seemed to know the danger before she did. She would be washing dishes and suddenly her shoulders would lock, her breathing would turn shallow, and only when the moment passed would she realize she had been smelling something—dish soap, maybe, or the faint metallic tang of tap water—that her mind had connected to the hospital.

Safety became a place. Moana could feel calm only in the corner of her living room where a certain armchair sat, or in the small back garden where the air smelled of jasmine and nothing else. She started waking at three or four in the morning, not with a start but with a quiet, certain alertness, as though her body was checking a perimeter. She would lie still, listening to Tanielu breathe, and count her own breaths until she was sure she was not suffocating. If she coughed even once, she got up and walked to that armchair, refusing to go back to bed until dawn.

The counterfactual thoughts came when she least expected them—while chopping vegetables, while watching television. She would find herself imagining a version of her life where the bacteria had never entered her lungs, where she had not cancelled that summer tour, where she was still the person who could belt a ballad without checking her air supply. That version of Moana did not lie awake fearing her own body. That Moana trusted herself. The real Moana had come to believe she could not trust a single decision she made, because if she had made the right ones, she would never have gotten sick in the first place.

It was Tanielu who finally said something, after she turned down a paid residency at a small venue. He did not push, but he asked gently: “When did you decide that you don't get to have your life back?” The question stayed with her. She started reading about trauma online, recognizing fragments of herself in the descriptions, though she resisted calling it that. A week later, she called a clinic and made an appointment. She was terrified—of what the therapist would think of her, of whether she would be able to talk without breaking down, of the possibility that she was too broken to fix. But she was also exhausted from the night-waking and the smallness of her world. She wanted to sing again. She wanted to stop feeling that she deserved her own suffering. She did not know if she could, but she showed up anyway, and that, for now, was enough.
